title: Polar Exploration Then & Now
keyIdea: The Heroic Age of polar exploration ran from 1897 to 1922. Teams used dog sledges, skis, wooden ships and a sextant to find their place from the Sun, with no radio on the ice, and many people died. Today polar scientists use GPS, satellites, ski planes, icebreaker ships and heated research stations. The questions are much the same: where am I, how cold is it, what was it like long ago? The tools are new. Ice cores read air from hundreds of thousands of years ago, and teams of women and men from many countries share what they find.
familyTip: Pick one thing you use every day, like a phone map or a warm coat. Ask: what would a 1911 explorer have used instead? Then look up one modern polar station, such as Halley VI, and spot three things that 1911 explorers did not have.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort 1911 kit from today's, race a sledge and a plane, match old questions to new tools, drill an ice core.

kid: From 1897 to 1922, teams set off for the coldest places on Earth. We call it the Heroic Age. They had dog sledges, skis, wooden ships and thick wool and fur. To find where they were, they used a sextant to measure how high the Sun was.

It was very risky. There was no radio on the ice, so no one could call for help. When Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911, the world did not hear for three months. Scott and four men died on the way back from the Pole.

Today scientists fly in on ski planes and live in heated stations. Halley VI even stands on legs with skis, so it can be moved. GPS tells them where they are to a few metres. Satellite phones let them call home.

The big questions are still the same. How cold is it? How thick is the ice? What was it like long ago? Ice cores answer the last one. Each year's snow traps a little air. Deeper ice is older, so a deep core holds air from about 800,000 years ago. The teams have changed too. In 1911 every team was all men, and each raced for its own country. In 1969 the first women reached the South Pole. Now scientists from more than 50 countries work together and share what they find.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This fits KS2 geography in the National Curriculum in England (locate the polar regions and describe their human and physical geography) and the KS2 science aim of working scientifically, using the Heroic Age (1897 to 1922, from the Belgica to Shackleton's death on the Quest) as the comparison. It builds on Brave Polar Explorers, which tells the race to the Pole for younger children; this lesson is about how and why polar work has changed.

The lab has five tasks. Learners sort eight items of kit into 1911 or today, and every wrong drop explains the date, such as GPS satellites from 1978 or dogs removed from Antarctica by 1994. They race a dog sledge (56 days for about 1,500 km) against a ski plane at about 300 km/h. They give four old science questions their modern tool, drill an ice core and order three samples by age with their carbon dioxide levels, and sort facts about teams then and now.

Common mistakes. Children often think Heroic Age teams only raced, when they also collected weather records and fossils: Scott's party hauled about 16 kg of rocks from the Beardmore Glacier. Many assume deeper ice is younger because it was found last. Watch, too, for the idea that only men do polar science, or that one country owns Antarctica; the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 keeps it for peace and science.

practice.prompt: Which of these did a 1911 explorer use to work out where they were?
practice.hint: Think about which of these needs a satellite.
practice.explain: A sextant measures how high the Sun is. GPS and satellite photos need satellites, and the first satellite went up in 1957.

practice.prompt: A dog team covers {d} km a day for {n} days. How far does it go, in km?
practice.hint: Multiply the distance each day by the number of days.
practice.explain: Each day adds {d} km, so {n} days give {d} × {n} = {=d*n} km. Amundsen's dogs managed about 27 km a day on the way to the Pole.

practice.prompt: An ice core has a layer from 1800 and a layer from the Ice Age. Which layer is deeper?
practice.hint: Snow piles up on top each year.
practice.explain: The Ice Age snow fell first, so newer snow piled on top of it. Older ice is deeper.

practice.prompt: A ski plane flies at {v} km/h for {h} hours. How far does it fly, in km?
practice.explain: Each hour the plane covers {v} km, so {h} hours give {v} × {h} = {=v*h} km. That is weeks of sledging in a few hours.

practice.prompt: Why do today's scientists not need to haul food on sledges all winter?
choices: Supplies are flown in to heated stations
practice.explain: Ski planes and ships bring supplies to heated research stations, so teams do not live in tents all season.

pool.prompt: Which is new since the Heroic Age?
pool.explain: Satellites did not exist until 1957, so a satellite phone is modern. Dog sledges and skis were Heroic Age kit.

pool.prompt: In 1911, how did news of reaching the South Pole get home?
choices: By ship and telegraph, months later
pool.hint: There was no radio on the ice.
pool.explain: Amundsen sailed to Hobart in Tasmania and sent the news by telegraph in March 1912, three months after reaching the Pole.

pool.prompt: A sledge team needs {n} days to reach the Pole and the same to come back. How many days is the whole trip?
pool.hint: There and back is two lots of the same trip.
pool.explain: The way back is as long as the way there, so the whole trip is {n} + {n} = {=2*n} days. Amundsen's round trip took 99 days.

pool.prompt: What do bubbles in an ice core tell scientists?
choices: What the air was like when the snow fell
pool.hint: What gets trapped when snow is squashed into ice?
pool.explain: Each bubble is a tiny sample of old air, so scientists can measure gases like carbon dioxide from long ago.

pool.prompt: Mo says Heroic Age explorers only raced and did no science. Is he right?
choices: No: they kept weather records and collected rocks and fossils
pool.hint: Think about what Scott's team carried back.
pool.explain: They did science too. Scott's party hauled about 16 kg of rocks with fossils from the Beardmore Glacier.

choices: Women and men from many countries
Only explorers racing to be first
pool.explain: More than 50 countries have joined the Antarctic Treaty, and women and men work side by side, for example the glaciologist Liz Thomas.

pool.prompt: Which tool lets scientists see how thick the ice is?
pool.hint: You need something that can see through the ice.
pool.explain: Radar sends radio waves down through the ice and times the echo from the rock below.

pool.prompt: Air in 1800 held about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide. Air today holds about {t} ppm. How much more is that?
pool.hint: Take away the old amount from today's.
